summary: Binary search is an efficient algorithm for finding an element in a sorted array by repeatedly dividing the search interval in half. It starts with two indices, L and R, and at each step, it compares the target value k with the middle element M of the current interval. If k is less than A[M], the search continues in the left half; otherwise, it continues in the right half. This process repeats until the interval is reduced to a single element, achieving a time complexity of O(log n). The implementation typically uses L = -1 and R = n to avoid boundary issues, with M calculated as (L + R) / 2. To handle edge cases like finding lower or upper bounds, the algorithm can be adapted by adjusting the conditions for updating L and R. It is crucial to avoid integer overflow when calculating M, which can be mitigated by using formulas like l + (r - l) / 2 or std::midpoint in C++20. Binary search can also be applied to monotonic functions or continuous real-valued functions by adapting the predicate used for comparison. Common mistakes include off-by-one errors, not accounting for negative bounds, and integer overflow, which must be carefully managed.
